Corrections recorded from real bug reports on this codebase (upstream GitHub issue numbers in

**What happened:** article responses never include `favorited`, so every RealWorld frontend

**Rule:** the RealWorld spec is the contract. Before calling an endpoint "done", diff its
response against the spec's object shape, not against what our own client happens to read.

### [LESSONS.md] LESSONS.md > Lessons Learned — RealWorld API (NestJS) > Static routes are declared before parameterised ones (#7)

`getFeed()` above `findOne()` in `ArticleController`.

**Rule:** in a controller, any literal path (`feed`, `popular`, `search`) goes above the `:slug`
handler. Order in the class is match order.

Handlers read `@Body('article')`, `@Body('user')`, `@Body('comment')` — the client sends
`{ "article": {...} }`, never a flat object. New endpoints follow the same nesting.

### [.claude/knowledge/workspace.md] workspace.md > RealWorld API (NestJS) — workspace overview > Conventions (these are the rules, not suggestions) > The response envelope and the `RO` suffix
`RO` means **Response Object**. Every controller method returns the RealWorld envelope, named
`<Thing>RO` in `*.interface.ts`:

| Endpoint family | Returns | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| single article | `ArticleRO` | `{ article: {...} }` |
| list | `ArticlesRO` | `{ articles: [...], articlesCount: n }` |
| comments | `CommentsRO` | `{ comments: [...] }` |
| user | `UserRO` | `{ user: {..., token} }` |
| profile | `ProfileRO` | `{ profile: {..., following} }` |

The frontends read `response.article.slug`, `response.user.token`, etc. A method that returns a
bare entity instead of the envelope breaks every RealWorld client (see `LESSONS.md`).

One module per RealWorld resource. Each module owns its controller, service, entity and DTOs.
Module files also own **which routes require auth** — see `auth.md`.

`controller → service → repository/entity`. Controllers do no business logic and never touch a
repository; services do. Cross-module data (e.g. the article service needs users and follows)
is reached by injecting that module's repository via `TypeOrmModule.forFeature([...])` in the
importing module — see `article.module.ts`.

**Nowhere.** The middleware answers "is this a valid user"; no service or controller method
compares the caller with the record's owner:

| Action | Ownership check |
|---|---|
| `PUT /articles/:slug` | none — `ArticleService.update(slug, body)` does `Object.assign(article, body)` and saves |
| `DELETE /articles/:slug` | none — `delete({slug})` |
| `DELETE /articles/:slug/comments/:id` | none — and comments have no author to compare against anyway |
| `DELETE /users/:slug` | none, and unguarded |
| `PUT /user` | implicitly the caller (`@User('id')`), fine |

text:
**Refined prompt:** Confirm whether the API actually permits a non-author to edit someone else's article — trace `PUT /api/articles/:slug` from route registration to the line that should compare caller vs. author, and report the exposure, the missing enforcement point, and whether it is reachable today.

Yes. It's possible, and it's not a mystery — any logged-in user can edit any article on your instance right now.

## The path a hostile caller takes

**1. Route is registered as "protected":** `src/article/article.module.ts:27` puts `PUT articles/:slug` behind `AuthMiddleware`.

**2. But that middleware only authenticates.** `src/user/auth.middleware.ts:17-24` verifies the JWT, loads the user, sets `req.user`, calls `next()`. It answers "is this *a* valid user," never "is this user allowed to touch *this* record."

**3. The controller drops the caller entirely:**

```ts
@Put(':slug')
async update(@Param() params, @Body('article') articleData: CreateArticleDto) {
  return this.articleService.update(params.slug, articleData);
}
```
`src/article/article.controller.ts:59-63` — note there's no `@User('id')` parameter at all. Compare `create()` at line 52, which *does* take `@User('id') userId`. The identity of the caller is available and simply isn't read.

**4. The service has nothing to compare with:**

```ts
async update(slug: string, articleData: any): Promise<ArticleRO> {
  let toUpdate = await this.articleRepository.findOne({ slug: slug});
  let updated = Object.assign(toUpdate, articleData);
  const article = await this.articleRepository.save(updated);
  return {article};
}
```
`src/article/article.service.ts:190-195` — it loads by slug, blind-assigns the body, saves. `article.author` is never loaded (`findOne` doesn't join it) and never checked.

## The enforcement point that should stop it

There is exactly one place it belongs: `ArticleService.update()` (article.service.ts:190), which needs the caller's id threaded from the controller, must load the article with its `author` relation, and must `throw new HttpException(..., HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN)` when `article.author.id !== userId`. No such line exists anywhere in the file.

The `@ApiResponse({ status: 403, description: 'Forbidden.' })` on article.controller.ts:58 describes intended behavior, not implemented behavior. Nothing in this codebase returns 403. That Swagger annotation is likely why this was assumed safe.

## Is it reachable?

**Yes, reachable today by any authenticated user.** The only precondition is a valid JWT — i.e. any registered account, including one the attacker signs up for themselves via `POST /api/users`. They need the target's slug, which `GET /api/articles` hands out publicly (article.controller.ts:24). No ownership barrier stands between that and the write.

Two aggravating details:
- `Object.assign(toUpdate, articleData)` (line 192) copies **whatever keys the body contains**, not just the DTO's fields. A crafted body can reach non-DTO columns like `favoriteCount`, or `authorId` — meaning an attacker can not only edit your article but reassign its authorship to themselves.
- `DELETE /articles/:slug` (controller.ts:68, service.ts:197) has the identical hole, and so does `DELETE /articles/:slug/comments/:id`.

## Two things I can't tell you from the code

Whether *this specific* edit was that exploit. There's no audit trail — `update()` logs nothing, and `article.updated` is bumped by `@BeforeUpdate()` without recording who did it. If you have reverse-proxy access logs, correlate the `PUT /api/articles/<your-slug>` timestamp against the `Authorization` bearer's subject; that's the only way to attribute it.

Also worth ruling out the mundane explanation first: a collaborator with legitimate access, or your own session on another device. The vulnerability being real doesn't prove it's what happened here.

---

This is item #2 on `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`'s active list ("Ownership checks on PUT/DELETE") and it's recorded in `LESSONS.md` as issues #6/#44 — so it's known, just not yet closed. Want me to write the fix for `PUT`/`DELETE /articles/:slug`? It's a contained change: thread `@User('id')` into both handlers, load the `author` relation in the service, and throw 403 on mismatch. The comment case is harder and should stay separate — `Comment` has no author column at all (`src/article/comment.entity.ts`), so there's nothing to compare against until that relation exists.
